alignment.note: Greek and Latin render the verb with an explicit conjunction plus future indicative (καὶ ἔσονται / et erunt); Syriac fuses the conjunction and the verb into a single morphological unit ܘܢܗܘܘܢ, a typical feature of Aramaic verbal morphology where the prefixed waw and the imperfect coalesce.

Greek supplies the article with the numeral (οἱ δύο, 'the two'); Latin and Syriac express 'the two' without an article — Latin lacks the article entirely, while Syriac ܬܪܝܗܘܢ carries the pronominal suffix -hon ('the two of them'), an inherent definiteness device.

Greek and Latin use the prepositional construction 'into/for one flesh' (εἰς σάρκα μίαν / in carne una); Syriac drops the preposition and renders a bare predicate 'one flesh' (ܚܕ ܒܣܪ), reflecting the Aramaic preference for nominal apposition over prepositional resultatives.

Greek compresses the negation into the single adverb οὐκέτι ('no longer'); Latin expands it analytically into jam non; Syriac uses the bare negative ܠܐ without an explicit 'longer' element, leaning on context to supply the temporal sense.

Greek and Latin use the present indicative (εἰσὶν / sunt, 'they are'); Syriac employs the perfect ܗܘܘ ('they were/have become'), a tense shift idiomatic in Aramaic where the perfect can express resultant present state.
μία σάρξ / ܚܕ ܒܣܪ / una caro — 'one flesh'.
